summary: Defines objects for the Management Information Base used to manage SONET and SDH interfaces. The text describes it as an experimental portion of the MIB. It was replaced by RFC 2558.

eli5.summary: A list of dials and gauges for checking a very fast fiber-optic link. A newer list replaced it.

subtitle: Monitoring very high-speed fiber-optic links with SNMP error counters and status

tldr.problem: Network operators need to monitor very high-speed fiber-optic links (SONET and SDH) to detect errors, failures, and performance degradation at different layers of the signal hierarchy.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1595 defines managed objects for Section, Line, Path, and Virtual Tributary layers that track error counts, defect conditions, alarm signals, and line status at each layer, including both current conditions and interval-based statistics.
tldr.outcome: Operators can use SNMP to check link health, identify which layer is failing, and measure quality. The MIB was replaced by RFC 2558 with refinements.

today: RFC 1595 is a Proposed Standard that defines objects for monitoring SONET and SDH links. It was obsoleted by RFC 2558.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 1595 defines a Management Information Base for SONET (Synchronous Optical Network) and SDH (Synchronous Digital Hierarchy) interfaces. These are standard protocols for transmitting data over fiber-optic cables at speeds of tens to hundreds of gigabits per second. SONET is used in North America; SDH is the equivalent standard used elsewhere. Both define the same layered signal hierarchy and similar monitoring objects.

A SONET/SDH link consists of multiple layers: the physical medium, the optical section (regenerator section), the line (multiplexing section), paths (end-to-end connections), and virtual tributaries or virtual containers (sub-multiplexed circuits). The MIB defines management objects for each layer to monitor errors and status independently.
sections.eli5: SONET and SDH are like super-fast postal systems that send data through fiber-optic cables. Each cable has multiple layers that stack on top of each other. This MIB has separate dials for each layer so you can see which one is broken.

sections.title: Layered Architecture
sections.content:
A SONET/SDH signal is organized in layers. At the bottom is the physical medium (the fiber itself). Above that is the Section layer (also called the regenerator section), which handles individual hops between regenerators. Next is the Line layer (which groups sections together). Then come Paths, which represent end-to-end connections across multiple lines. Finally, Virtual Tributaries (in SONET) or Virtual Containers (in SDH) are lower-rate circuits multiplexed inside a path—for example, a 155 Mbps path might carry 28 lower-speed circuits.

Different equipment terminates different layers. A regenerator only processes the section layer. An add-drop multiplexer (ADM) processes the line layer. A terminal multiplexer processes paths and virtual tributaries. The MIB lets operators monitor each layer independently, so they can pinpoint which layer has the problem.
sections.eli5: Think of a highway system. Each layer is like a different road level: the ground is the fiber, then come different highway sections, then routes across sections, then local roads branching off. Each level can be monitored separately.

sections.title: Error Detection and Defects
sections.content:
SONET/SDH defines specific error conditions at each layer. Loss of Signal (LOS) is detected when the incoming signal has no transitions. Loss of Frame (LOF) is declared after a loss-of-signal condition persists for several milliseconds, and Loss of Pointer (LOP) occurs when a path pointer is not found.

The MIB tracks Coding Violations (CV)—bit errors detected by parity checks—separately at each layer. At each layer, an Errored Second (ES) is any second with one or more CVs or defects. A Severely Errored Second (SES) is a second with a high error count or a defect present. Unavailable Seconds count periods when the interface is down due to persistent errors. The RFC defines specific thresholds for SES at each layer and rate.
sections.eli5: The system watches for different kinds of problems: no signal at all, lost timing, bit errors, and corrupted packets. It counts how many seconds had problems and how many bits got corrupted.

sections.title: Alarm Signals
sections.content:
When something goes wrong at one layer, the downstream equipment needs to know. Alarm Indication Signals (AIS) are sent by a terminating equipment when it detects a failure, so the receiving equipment knows not to expect good data. Remote Defect Indication (RDI, sometimes called FERF, Far-End Remote Failure) tells upstream equipment that the far end has detected a problem on the return path.

Different AIS types exist at different layers: Line AIS, STS-Path AIS, and VT-Path AIS. The MIB tracks whether these signals are present. Signal Label Mismatches occur when a path or virtual tributary is not correctly configured. Unequipped signals indicate a path or VT is not provisioned. The Circuit Identifier is a text string provided by the equipment vendor for troubleshooting.
sections.eli5: When one part of the system breaks, it sends messages downstream saying "I am broken, do not believe what I send." The system counts when these warning messages are sent and received.

sections.title: Current and Interval Statistics
sections.content:
For each layer (Section, Line, Path, and Virtual Tributary), the MIB defines two sets of objects. The Current group reports real-time status and counters since the interface came up or since the last interval boundary (whichever is more recent). This includes current defects, current status, and accumulated error counts.

The Interval group provides statistics collected over fixed 15-minute windows. Each interval records its own error counts, SES and UAS totals, and validity flags. A validity flag indicates whether data in that interval is complete (some equipment resets counters on configuration changes). Storing multiple intervals lets operators see trends: for example, if the same interval every day has high error counts, it may indicate a scheduled backup or test.
sections.eli5: The system keeps two kinds of records: what is happening right now, and what happened in each 15-minute block. The 15-minute records show patterns that repeat every day or week.

sections.title: Far-End Statistics
sections.content:
SONET/SDH protocols include overhead bytes in which the far end can report status back toward the transmitter. The Far End objects report what the distant equipment is telling us about the signal it receives. For the Line and Path layers, the MIB includes both Near-End (what we see locally) and Far-End (what the other end reports) statistics.

Far-End statistics are useful because they let you distinguish between problems on your equipment, problems on the line itself, and problems on the far end's equipment. If the Near-End counters are low but Far-End counters are high, the issue is probably on your receiving equipment or the transmission line toward you. If Near-End is high but Far-End is low, the issue is likely on the far end or the line toward them.
sections.eli5: The far end sends back a report card saying "I got this many bit errors from you." By comparing what we see locally and what they see, you can tell where the problem really is.
